explanation: The subxiphoid needle angled toward the pericardial sac depicts pericardiocentesis, which aspirates effusion fluid to relieve tamponade or obtain diagnostic samples.

imageRef: rednd-229_Brick Exchange - Peripheral Arterial Disease_p10_1.png
label: Ankle-brachial index
explanation: Dividing ankle systolic pressure by brachial systolic pressure gives the ABI. A reduced ratio (typically <0.9) signals arterial obstruction, confirming peripheral arterial disease.

imageRef: rednd-230_Brick Exchange - Peripheral Arterial Disease_p18_1.png
label: Stent placement
explanation: The panels depict balloon angioplasty with placement of a balloon-expandable stent: the balloon dilates the stenosis and the expanded stent provides a permanent scaffold that resists elastic recoil and keeps the lumen open.

imageRef: rednd-231_Brick Exchange - Peripheral Arterial Disease_p19_1.png
label: Endarterectomy
explanation: The artery is opened longitudinally and the atherosclerotic plaque is being dissected free from the wall, which is the defining step of an endarterectomy performed to restore blood flow through a clogged artery.

imageRef: rednd-232_Brick Exchange - Peripheral Arterial Disease_p20_1.png
label: Vein graft bypass
explanation: A vein graft is anastomosed above and below the occluded artery, creating a bypass channel that carries blood past the blockage and restores perfusion to the distal limb.

imageRef: rednd-233_Brick Exchange - Physiology- Alveolar Gas exchange and Diffusion 2 of 2_p2_1.png
label: Respiratory membrane
brick: Physiology- Alveolar Gas exchange and Diffusion 2 of 2
explanation: Gas diffusion is inversely proportional to membrane thickness (Fick's law). Thickening any layer of the respiratory membrane, as with pulmonary edema or fibrosis, lengthens the diffusion path and reduces O2/CO2 transfer.

imageRef: rednd-234_Brick Exchange - Physiology- Alveolar Gas exchange and Diffusion 2 of 2_p6_1.png
label: Alveolar gas exchange
brick: Physiology- Alveolar Gas exchange and Diffusion 2 of 2
explanation: Gas exchange at the alveolus is passive diffusion driven by the partial pressure difference (ΔP) across the membrane. O2 diffuses down its gradient into the capillary, where it is rapidly bound by hemoglobin during RBC uptake, keeping the gradient favorable as blood flows through.

imageRef: rednd-235_Brick Exchange - Physiology_ Mechanics and pressures of breathing_p4_1.png
label: Respiratory muscles
brick: Physiology: Mechanics and pressures of breathing
explanation: The diaphragm is the principal muscle of inspiration; its contraction flattens the dome, increasing thoracic volume and lowering intrathoracic pressure to draw air in. Scalenes and sternocleidomastoid are accessory inspiratory muscles used with increased effort, while the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles (rectus abdominis, obliques) drive active/forced expiration.

imageRef: rednd-236_Brick Exchange - Pleural Effusion_p13_1.png
label: Pleural effusion
explanation: A large volume of pleural fluid produces a homogeneous opacity that obscures the lung and diaphragm, with a characteristic meniscus (concave superior margin) as fluid tracks up the lateral chest wall. Massive effusions can white-out the hemithorax; if under tension they may push the mediastinum away from the affected side.

imageRef: rednd-237_Brick Exchange - Pleural Effusion_p17_1.png
label: Thoracentesis
explanation: Thoracentesis is performed with the patient upright and leaning forward so that fluid pools posteriorly and inferiorly; a needle is introduced above a rib into the pleural space to withdraw the effusion for diagnostic analysis or symptomatic relief.

imageRef: rednd-238_Brick Exchange - Pneumoconioses_p11_1.png
label: Silicotic nodule
explanation: The silicotic nodule is characterized by concentric ('onion-skin') layers of hyalinized collagen. Polarized light reveals birefringent silica particles within it. These nodules coalesce over time and can progress to massive fibrosis.

imageRef: rednd-239_Brick Exchange - Pneumoconioses_p13_1.png
label: Asbestos bodies
explanation: Asbestos bodies are ferruginous bodies: thin asbestos fibers coated with an iron-containing proteinaceous material, producing golden-brown beaded rods with knobbed ends. Their presence indicates significant asbestos exposure.

imageRef: rednd-240_Brick Exchange - Pneumoconioses_p7_1.png
label: Anthracosis
explanation: Inhaled carbon/coal dust is engulfed by macrophages, producing black anthracotic pigment. Accumulation around bronchioles and in interstitium underlies coal workers' pneumoconiosis (anthracosis when asymptomatic).

imageRef: rednd-241_Brick Exchange - Pneumothorax_p14_1.png
label: Tension pneumothorax
explanation: Tension pneumothorax occurs when a one-way air leak progressively raises intrapleural pressure, shifting the mediastinum/trachea toward the contralateral side, impeding venous return (distended neck veins, hypotension), and causing hyperresonance with absent breath sounds. It requires immediate needle decompression.

imageRef: rednd-242_Brick Exchange - Pneumothorax_p20_1.png
label: Subcutaneous emphysema
explanation: The ginkgo-leaf sign is caused by free gas (subcutaneous emphysema) dissecting between the fibers of the pectoralis major, here associated with a right pneumothorax marked by a visible pleural edge.

imageRef: rednd-243_Brick Exchange - Pneumothorax_p26_1.png
label: Chest drainage system
explanation: The water seal bottle is a one-way valve: air from the pleural space bubbles out through the submerged tube but water prevents atmospheric air from being drawn back in. The pressure-regulating bottle sets suction and the collection bottle traps fluid.

imageRef: rednd-244_Brick Exchange - Pneumothorax_p28_1.png
label: Pigtail catheter
explanation: Small-bore pigtail catheters effectively evacuate air with less pain than large-bore tubes and are well suited to simple pneumothorax; viscous or particulate collections (blood, pus, clot) require a larger-bore chest tube.

imageRef: rednd-245_Brick Exchange - Pneumothorax_p2_1.png
label: Chest radiograph
explanation: This is a standing PA chest radiograph, showing the ribs, lungs, mediastinum, and hemidiaphragms with the characteristic grayscale of plain film.

imageRef: rednd-246_Brick Exchange - Pneumothorax_p5_1.png
label: Pneumothorax
explanation: The lung is normally held open by negative intrapleural pressure. When air enters the pleural space this negative pressure is lost, the lung's elastic recoil is unopposed, and it collapses inward.

imageRef: rednd-247_Brick Exchange - Pneumothorax_p8_1.png
label: Bleb
explanation: The pale, thin-walled outpouching on the visceral pleural surface is a bleb/bulla; rupture of such lesions is the usual cause of spontaneous pneumothorax and they are often stapled/resected at VATS.

imageRef: rednd-248_Brick Exchange - Pressure Volume (PV) Loops_p8_1.png
label: Pressure-volume loop
explanation: The area enclosed by the ventricular pressure-volume loop equals the external stroke work of the left ventricle; the width of the loop is stroke volume (EDV-ESV).

imageRef: rednd-249_Brick Exchange - Primary (Essential) Hypertension_p5_1.png
label: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
explanation: The diagram depicts the RAAS: renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, pulmonary ACE converts it to angiotensin II, which drives vasoconstriction and aldosterone-mediated Na/water retention.

imageRef: rednd-250_Brick Exchange - Pulmonary Circulation_p15_1.png
label: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction
explanation: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction shunts blood away from hypoxic alveoli toward well-oxygenated regions, optimizing ventilation-perfusion matching.

imageRef: rednd-251_Brick Exchange - Pulmonary Circulation_p23_1.png
label: Pulmonary edema
explanation: Fluid leaving the capillary first accumulates in the interstitium/perivascular space and then floods the alveoli, the sequence of pulmonary edema formation.

imageRef: rednd-252_Brick Exchange - Pulmonary Circulation_p7_1.png
label: West lung zones
explanation: In West Zone 1 (alveolar > arterial > venous pressure), alveolar pressure compresses the capillaries and no flow occurs; this zone is normally absent in healthy people.

imageRef: rednd-253_Brick Exchange - Pulmonary Function Tests (PFT)_p10_1.png
label: Flow-volume loop
explanation: The flow-volume loop is produced during spirometry; the peak of the expiratory limb is the peak expiratory flow and the width of the loop spans the vital capacity.

imageRef: rednd-254_Brick Exchange - Pulmonary Function Tests (PFT)_p6_1.png
label: Spirometry
explanation: The handheld mouthpiece connected to a recording unit that plots volume-time and flow-volume loops is a spirometer. Spirometry measures forced expiratory volumes and flows (e.g., FEV1, FVC) to characterize obstructive versus restrictive patterns.

imageRef: rednd-255_Brick Exchange - Pulmonary Ventilation and Perfusion (V_Q)_p7_1.png
label: West lung zones
explanation: These are the West zones. In zone 1 (apex) alveolar pressure > arterial > venous (PA>Pa>Pv), so alveolar pressure compresses capillaries and flow is minimal. Zone 3 (base) has Pa>Pv>PA with continuous flow.

imageRef: rednd-256_Brick Exchange - Respiratory Alkalosis_p11_1.png
label: Pulmonary embolism
explanation: On CT pulmonary angiography, hypodense (dark) filling defects within the contrast-opacified pulmonary arteries indicate thromboemboli. Large central emboli can cause hyperventilation and a secondary respiratory alkalosis.

imageRef: rednd-257_Brick Exchange - Respiratory_ Alveolar ventilation and Dead space 1 of 2_p4_1.png
label: Oxygen cascade
brick: Respiratory: Alveolar ventilation and Dead space 1 of 2
explanation: The stepwise decline in PO2 from inspired air through humidification, alveolar dilution, diffusion, venous admixture, and tissue diffusion down to mitochondria is the oxygen cascade—the sequential pressure drops driving O2 from atmosphere to cells.

imageRef: rednd-258_Brick Exchange - Respiratory_ Alveolar ventilation and Dead space 1 of 2_p7_1.png
label: Alveolar gas equation
brick: Respiratory: Alveolar ventilation and Dead space 1 of 2
explanation: This is the alveolar gas equation. Solving for alveolar PO2 (PAO2) and subtracting measured arterial PO2 (PaO2) yields the A-a gradient, which helps distinguish causes of hypoxemia (e.g., shunt/V-Q mismatch versus hypoventilation).

imageRef: rednd-259_Brick Exchange - Respiratory_ B. pertussis and C. diphtheriae_p11_1.png
label: Elek test
brick: Respiratory: B. pertussis and C. diphtheriae
explanation: This is the Elek test, an immunodiffusion assay. Antitoxin diffusing from the filter paper meets toxin from a toxigenic strain, forming precipitin lines; a non-toxigenic strain produces none. It confirms toxin production rather than mere isolation.

imageRef: rednd-260_Brick Exchange - Respiratory_ B. pertussis and C. diphtheriae_p19_1.png
label: Bordetella pertussis
brick: Respiratory: B. pertussis and C. diphtheriae
explanation: Bordetella pertussis is a small, fastidious Gram-negative coccobacillus that stains faintly. It causes whooping cough with the characteristic catarrhal, paroxysmal, and convalescent stages; toxin-mediated ciliary damage produces the severe coughing paroxysms.

imageRef: rednd-261_Brick Exchange - Respiratory_ B. pertussis and C. diphtheriae_p2_1.png
label: Corynebacterium diphtheriae
brick: Respiratory: B. pertussis and C. diphtheriae
explanation: Corynebacterium diphtheriae is a Gram-positive, club-shaped bacillus that divides to form V- and Y-shaped 'Chinese letter' arrangements. Its exotoxin (ADP-ribosylates EF-2) causes the pseudomembranous pharyngitis and systemic toxicity of diphtheria.

imageRef: rednd-262_Brick Exchange - Respiratory_ B. pertussis and C. diphtheriae_p4_2.png
label: Diphtheritic pseudomembrane
brick: Respiratory: B. pertussis and C. diphtheriae
explanation: The diphtheritic pseudomembrane is a tough, adherent gray coagulum of fibrin, necrotic epithelium, leukocytes, and bacteria. It bleeds on removal and can extend to obstruct the airway, a hallmark of respiratory diphtheria.

imageRef: rednd-263_Brick Exchange - Respiratory_ B. pertussis and C. diphtheriae_p5_1.png
label: Bull neck
brick: Respiratory: B. pertussis and C. diphtheriae
explanation: Severe diphtheria causes prominent cervical lymphadenopathy with surrounding soft-tissue edema, producing the characteristic 'bull neck.' It signals extensive toxin-mediated disease and portends airway compromise and systemic toxicity.

imageRef: rednd-264_Brick Exchange - Respiratory_ B. pertussis and C. diphtheriae_p9_1.png
label: Metachromatic granules
brick: Respiratory: B. pertussis and C. diphtheriae
explanation: Corynebacterium diphtheriae stores polyphosphate as metachromatic (Babes-Ernst/volutin) granules that stain a contrasting color at the cell poles with stains such as Albert or Neisser, aiding presumptive identification.

imageRef: rednd-265_Brick Exchange - Respiratory_ Carbon Monoxide (CO) Poisoning and Cyanide (CN) Poisoning_p13_1.png
label: Pulse CO-oximeter
brick: Respiratory: Carbon Monoxide (CO) Poisoning and Cyanide (CN) Poisoning
explanation: A pulse CO-oximeter uses multiple light wavelengths to distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, allowing noninvasive detection of CO poisoning. A standard 2-wavelength pulse oximeter cannot, and reads falsely normal SpO2 in CO poisoning.

imageRef: rednd-266_Brick Exchange - Restrictive Cardiomyopathy_p10_1.png
label: Cardiac amyloidosis
explanation: Cardiac amyloidosis deposits amorphous, eosinophilic, acellular protein in the interstitium and around myocytes, stiffening the ventricle and producing a restrictive cardiomyopathy with impaired diastolic filling.

imageRef: rednd-267_Brick Exchange - Restrictive Cardiomyopathy_p11_1.png
label: Congo red birefringence
explanation: Congo red stains amyloid, which shows pathognomonic apple-green birefringence under polarized light due to the beta-pleated sheet structure. This confirms cardiac amyloidosis as the cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy.

imageRef: rednd-268_Brick Exchange - Restrictive Cardiomyopathy_p11_2.png
label: Cardiac sarcoidosis
explanation: Cardiac sarcoidosis produces noncaseating granulomas in the myocardium that can cause conduction blocks, arrhythmias, and a restrictive/infiltrative cardiomyopathy. Granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid histiocytes distinguishes it from bland fibrosis.

imageRef: rednd-269_Brick Exchange - Restrictive Cardiomyopathy_p12_1.png
label: Prussian blue iron stain
explanation: The Prussian blue (Perls) reaction stains ferric iron blue. Myocardial iron overload in hereditary hemochromatosis or transfusional siderosis causes a restrictive/dilated cardiomyopathy; the triad of diabetes, skin pigmentation, and organ deposition is classic.

imageRef: rednd-270_Brick Exchange - Restrictive Cardiomyopathy_p14_1.png
label: Cardiac MRI
explanation: Cardiac MRI provides tissue characterization; late gadolinium enhancement patterns and T1/T2 mapping help identify infiltrative and inflammatory causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy such as amyloid, sarcoid, and fibrosis.

imageRef: rednd-271_Brick Exchange - ST Segment Changes_ Recognition and Localization of Myocardial Ischemia_p3_1.png
label: J point
brick: ST Segment Changes: Recognition and Localization of Myocardial Ischemia
explanation: The J point is where the QRS complex ends and the ST segment begins; it is the reference used to measure ST elevation or depression relative to the baseline (T-P segment).

imageRef: rednd-272_Brick Exchange - Sarcoidosis_p13_1.png
label: Erythema nodosum
explanation: Erythema nodosum is a septal panniculitis producing tender red nodules on the shins; in sarcoidosis its presence with bilateral hilar adenopathy and arthritis constitutes Lofgren syndrome and carries a good prognosis.

imageRef: rednd-273_Brick Exchange - Secondary Hypertension_p12_1.png
label: Cushing syndrome
explanation: Chronic glucocorticoid excess (Cushing syndrome) produces moon face, buffalo hump, central obesity with striae, thin skin, proximal myopathy, and osteoporosis; excess cortisol also raises blood pressure, causing secondary hypertension.

imageRef: rednd-274_Brick Exchange - Secondary Hypertension_p15_1.png
label: Obstructive sleep apnea
explanation: During sleep, relaxation of pharyngeal muscles lets the tongue and soft palate collapse posteriorly, occluding the upper airway. This is obstructive sleep apnea, a recognized secondary cause of hypertension.

imageRef: rednd-275_Brick Exchange - Secondary Hypertension_p7_1.png
label: Fibromuscular dysplasia
explanation: Fibromuscular dysplasia causes non-atherosclerotic thickening of the arterial wall, giving a beaded appearance with intervening stenoses. It predominantly affects young to middle-aged women and is a treatable cause of secondary hypertension.

imageRef: rednd-276_Brick Exchange - Secondary Hypertension_p8_1.png
label: Renal artery stenosis
explanation: Reduced perfusion pressure from renal artery stenosis is sensed by the juxtaglomerular apparatus, triggering renin release and downstream angiotensin II/aldosterone activation, which drives renovascular hypertension.

imageRef: rednd-277_Brick Exchange - Secondary Hypertension_p9_1.png
label: Fibromuscular dysplasia
explanation: The alternating areas of stenosis and dilation give a classic 'string of beads' pattern on angiography, diagnostic of fibromuscular dysplasia of the renal artery.

imageRef: rednd-278_Brick Exchange - Sinus Bradycardia and Related Disorders_p14_1.png
label: Junctional rhythm
explanation: When the SA node fails, an AV-junctional pacemaker takes over. Because the impulse originates near the AV node, the QRS stays narrow but P waves are absent or buried, producing a junctional escape rhythm.

imageRef: rednd-279_Brick Exchange - Small-Vessel Vasculitis_p11_1.png
label: Palpable purpura
explanation: Raised, palpable purpura that does not blanch reflects inflammatory damage and leakage of postcapillary venules, the hallmark of small-vessel (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis, distinguishing it from flat non-palpable purpura seen with pure platelet defects.

imageRef: rednd-280_Brick Exchange - Small-Vessel Vasculitis_p8_1.png
label: Nasal polyps
explanation: Nasal polyps are edematous outgrowths of chronically inflamed sinonasal mucosa; when they obstruct a sinus ostium, mucus accumulates and impairs drainage, as shown.

imageRef: rednd-281_Brick Exchange - Starling Forces_p19_1.png
label: Pitting edema
explanation: When fingertip pressure displaces excess interstitial fluid and leaves a lingering depression, the edema is 'pitting,' typically reflecting increased capillary filtration (e.g., elevated hydrostatic pressure or low plasma oncotic pressure).

imageRef: rednd-282_Brick Exchange - Superficial Venous Disease_p10_1.png
label: Superficial thrombophlebitis
explanation: Trauma from an indwelling catheter injures the venous endothelium, promoting inflammation and clot formation within a superficial vein, i.e., superficial thrombophlebitis, typically presenting as a tender, red, cord-like vessel.

imageRef: rednd-283_Brick Exchange - Superficial Venous Disease_p13_1.png
label: Superficial thrombophlebitis
explanation: A palpable, tender, red cord following a superficial vein reflects thrombosis with surrounding inflammation of that vein (superficial thrombophlebitis), distinct from the diffuse swelling of DVT or the septal panniculitis of erythema nodosum.

imageRef: rednd-284_Brick Exchange - Superficial Venous Disease_p2_1.png
label: Chronic venous insufficiency
explanation: Long-standing venous hypertension from valvular incompetence produces dependent edema, skin thickening, and hemosiderin/pigment changes of the lower leg, the hallmark of chronic venous insufficiency.

imageRef: rednd-285_Brick Exchange - Superficial Venous Disease_p4_1.png
label: Stasis dermatitis
explanation: Chronic venous hypertension causes red-cell extravasation; breakdown of hemoglobin deposits hemosiderin, giving the characteristic brown pigmentation and eczematous change of stasis dermatitis in the gaiter area.

imageRef: rednd-286_Brick Exchange - Superficial Venous Disease_p6_1.png
label: Varicose vein
explanation: Sustained venous reflux dilates superficial veins into the visible, tortuous, elongated cords known as varicose veins.

imageRef: rednd-287_Brick Exchange - Superficial Venous Disease_p7_1.png
label: Lipodermatosclerosis
explanation: Chronic venous hypertension drives fibrosis of dermis and subcutaneous fat, producing the firm, hyperpigmented, inverted-champagne-bottle change called lipodermatosclerosis, often preceding venous ulceration.

imageRef: rednd-288_Brick Exchange - Superficial Venous Disease_p8_1.png
label: Sclerotherapy
explanation: Sclerotherapy injects a chemical sclerosant into the target vein, damaging the endothelium so the vein fibroses and is obliterated, as shown by the occluded lumen.

imageRef: rednd-289_Brick Exchange - Superficial Venous Disease_p9_1.png
label: Endovenous ablation
explanation: Endovenous thermal (radiofrequency or laser) ablation delivers heat that denatures the vein wall collagen, causing contraction and fibrotic closure as the catheter is slowly withdrawn.

imageRef: rednd-290_Brick Exchange - Tobacco Smoking_p3_1.png
label: E-cigarette
explanation: The pod-style form factor with a mouthpiece identifies an electronic cigarette, which aerosolizes a nicotine-containing liquid for inhalation.

imageRef: rednd-291_Brick Exchange - Traumatic Injuries and other Disorders of the Chest Wall, Pleura, Mediastinum, and Lung_p11_1.png
label: Triangle of safety
brick: Traumatic Injuries and other Disorders of the Chest Wall, Pleura, Mediastinum, and Lung
explanation: The triangle bounded by pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, and a line at the 5th intercostal space (nipple level) is the safe zone for tube thoracostomy, avoiding major vessels, the heart, and abdominal organs.

imageRef: rednd-292_Brick Exchange - Traumatic Injuries and other Disorders of the Chest Wall, Pleura, Mediastinum, and Lung_p13_1.png
label: Pneumomediastinum
brick: Traumatic Injuries and other Disorders of the Chest Wall, Pleura, Mediastinum, and Lung
explanation: Air tracking along the mediastinal and cardiac borders (with the accompanying continuous diaphragm sign and neck/chest-wall lucencies of subcutaneous emphysema) indicates pneumomediastinum, air within the mediastinal soft tissues, often from alveolar or airway rupture in trauma.

imageRef: rednd-293_Brick Exchange - Traumatic Injuries and other Disorders of the Chest Wall, Pleura, Mediastinum, and Lung_p17_1.png
label: Tension pneumothorax
brick: Traumatic Injuries and other Disorders of the Chest Wall, Pleura, Mediastinum, and Lung
explanation: A hyperlucent hemithorax lacking peripheral vascular markings with contralateral mediastinal shift indicates a pneumothorax under tension, a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate needle decompression.

imageRef: rednd-294_Brick Exchange - Traumatic Injuries and other Disorders of the Chest Wall, Pleura, Mediastinum, and Lung_p3_1.png
label: Flail chest
brick: Traumatic Injuries and other Disorders of the Chest Wall, Pleura, Mediastinum, and Lung
explanation: A flail chest occurs when three or more contiguous ribs are each fractured in at least two locations, creating a free segment that moves inward on inspiration (paradoxical motion); it is frequently accompanied by underlying pulmonary contusion.

imageRef: rednd-295_Brick Exchange - Traumatic Injuries and other Disorders of the Chest Wall, Pleura, Mediastinum, and Lung_p5_1.png
label: Diaphragmatic rupture
brick: Traumatic Injuries and other Disorders of the Chest Wall, Pleura, Mediastinum, and Lung
explanation: Displacement of abdominal contents into the thoracic cavity through a defect in the diaphragm indicates traumatic diaphragmatic rupture, which most often affects the left hemidiaphragm and requires surgical repair.

imageRef: rednd-296_Brick Exchange - Traumatic Injuries and other Disorders of the Chest Wall, Pleura, Mediastinum, and Lung_p9_1.png
label: Chylothorax
brick: Traumatic Injuries and other Disorders of the Chest Wall, Pleura, Mediastinum, and Lung
explanation: A milky-white, triglyceride-rich pleural effusion is a chylothorax, caused by disruption of the thoracic duct (e.g., trauma or malignancy) allowing lymphatic chyle to accumulate in the pleural space.

imageRef: rednd-297_Brick Exchange - Tricuspid Regurgitation and Tricuspid Stenosis_p12_1.png
label: Jugular venous distension
explanation: The prominent distended vein coursing up the neck represents elevated jugular venous pressure (distension), a sign of systemic venous congestion seen with right-sided heart failure and severe tricuspid regurgitation.

imageRef: rednd-298_Brick Exchange - Tricuspid Regurgitation and Tricuspid Stenosis_p20_1.png
label: Echocardiogram
explanation: The grayscale sector image with a real-time color Doppler overlay (blue/red flow), frame rate, and depth annotations is characteristic of two-dimensional echocardiography. Here color Doppler reveals turbulent flow across a domed, stenotic tricuspid valve.

imageRef: rednd-299_Brick Exchange - Tricuspid Regurgitation and Tricuspid Stenosis_p2_1.png
label: Tricuspid valve
explanation: The valve has anterior, septal, and inferior (posterior) leaflets with intervening commissures and lies adjacent to the AV node region and encircled by the right coronary artery, identifying the right atrioventricular (tricuspid) valve.

imageRef: rednd-300_Brick Exchange - Vasculature and Lymphatics of the Heart_p3_1.png
label: Coronary artery
brick: Vasculature and Lymphatics of the Heart
explanation: The epicardial vessel coursing in a groove and sending penetrating branches deep into the myocardium to perfuse it is a coronary artery. Coronary arteries lie in the epicardial fat and give off intramural branches.

imageRef: rednd-301_Brick Exchange - Vasculature and Lymphatics of the Heart_p3_2.png
label: Coronary artery
brick: Vasculature and Lymphatics of the Heart
explanation: The boxed region highlights an epicardial coronary artery running over the surface of the heart within the epicardial fat, the vessels that supply the myocardium with oxygenated blood.

imageRef: rednd-302_Brick Exchange - Vasculature and Lymphatics of the Heart_p6_1.png
label: Coronary angiogram
brick: Vasculature and Lymphatics of the Heart
explanation: Selective injection of iodinated contrast into a coronary ostium with fluoroscopic imaging is coronary angiography, the gold standard for defining coronary anatomy and stenoses.

imageRef: rednd-303_Brick Exchange - Ventricular Arrhythmias_p10_1.png
label: Ventricular tachycardia
explanation: A regular wide-complex (broad QRS) tachycardia at a fast rate is ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise, arising from an ectopic ventricular focus below the AV node.

imageRef: rednd-304_Brick Exchange - Ventricular Arrhythmias_p12_1.png
label: Pacemaker
explanation: The device is a cardiac pacemaker: a pulse generator delivers electrical impulses through transvenous leads to the atrium and ventricle, triggering myocardial depolarization to maintain an adequate heart rate.

imageRef: rednd-305_Brick Exchange - Ventricular Arrhythmias_p17_1.png
label: Torsades de pointes
explanation: A polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with QRS complexes that appear to twist around the isoelectric baseline is torsades de pointes, classically associated with QT prolongation.

imageRef: rednd-306_Brick Exchange - Ventricular Arrhythmias_p7_2.png
label: Ventricular fibrillation
explanation: Chaotic, irregular waveforms without discrete QRS complexes represent ventricular fibrillation, a disorganized quivering of the ventricles that produces no cardiac output and requires immediate defibrillation.
